title: The Little People of the Forest

pages.text: One evening, Kwamla sat with Nana Akyaa under the neem tree. The forest grew dark beyond the farm. “Nana, are there little people in the forest?” he asked.
sentences: One evening, Kwamla sat with Nana Akyaa under the neem tree.
The forest grew dark beyond the farm.
“Nana, are there little people in the forest?” he asked.
pages.alt: Kwamla and his grandmother Nana Akyaa sitting on low wooden stools under a leafy neem tree in a village courtyard at dusk, with a dark green forest beyond the farm.

pages.text: Nana smiled. “Elders in our part of Ghana tell of the mmoatia, the little people of the forest. A Twi dictionary calls them short mythical creatures, or fairies, from Akan folklore. I tell you what we are told. It is a story we keep.”
sentences: Nana smiled.
“Elders in our part of Ghana tell of the mmoatia, the little people of the forest.
A Twi dictionary calls them short mythical creatures, or fairies, from Akan folklore.
I tell you what we are told.
It is a story we keep.”
pages.alt: Nana Akyaa speaking gently with warm expressive hands while Kwamla leans forward on his stool listening closely under the evening sky.

pages.text: Kwamla’s eyes grew wide. “Some people say a person was taken by them and came back with special powers.” Nana nodded. “People do say such things. I have seen no proof, so I tell it as a story and a belief, not as something I can show you.”
sentences: Kwamla’s eyes grew wide.
“Some people say a person was taken by them and came back with special powers.” Nana nodded.
“People do say such things.
I have seen no proof, so I tell it as a story and a belief, not as something I can show you.”
pages.alt: Close view of Kwamla looking wide-eyed and curious while Nana Akyaa nods thoughtfully with a calm, honest expression.

pages.text: “Then what do we do in the forest?” asked Kwamla. “We do what is true and safe,” said Nana. “We walk with grown-ups, we do not go in at night, and we respect the trees and the animals.”
sentences: “Then what do we do in the forest?” asked Kwamla.
“We do what is true and safe,” said Nana.
“We walk with grown-ups, we do not go in at night, and we respect the trees and the animals.”
pages.alt: Nana Akyaa pointing calmly toward a sunlit-dusk footpath at the edge of the tall forest trees while Kwamla looks toward the path attentively.

pages.text: Kwamla thought of a girl at school who was short. “Ewuradjoa is not one of the mmoatia, Nana,” he said. “Of course not,” said Nana. “She is a child, just like you. Stories belong to the forest. They never belong to our classmates.”
sentences: Kwamla thought of a girl at school who was short.
“Ewuradjoa is not one of the mmoatia, Nana,” he said.
“Of course not,” said Nana.
“She is a child, just like you.
Stories belong to the forest.
They never belong to our classmates.”
pages.alt: Kwamla and Nana Akyaa talking earnestly face to face under the warm glow of a courtyard lantern, Nana resting a gentle hand on Kwamla’s shoulder.

pages.text: Kwamla went to bed with two clear thoughts. One was the old story, which he would keep and tell. The other was the truth he knew for certain: every child is a person, and a person is never a spirit.
sentences: Kwamla went to bed with two clear thoughts.
One was the old story, which he would keep and tell.
The other was the truth he knew for certain: every child is a person, and a person is never a spirit.
pages.alt: Kwamla tucked peacefully under a patterned blanket in his cosy bedroom at night, smiling thoughtfully as a bright crescent moon and stars shine outside the open window.

activities.question: How does Nana tell the story of the mmoatia?
options: As a story and a belief

activities.question: What does Nana say about classmates?
options: Stories never belong to our classmates

items: Kwamla asks about the little people.
Nana tells the belief as a belief.
Nana says how to stay safe in the forest.
Nana says every classmate is a person.

activities.definition: The traditional stories and beliefs of a community.

activities.prompt: How do you feel when someone is teased about how they look?

glossary.definition: Little forest people in Akan folklore (told as a belief, not proven fact).
To treat someone or something with care and honour.
Something that people hold to be true, even when it cannot be proven.
